blocks.x: All right, today is Tuesday, March 25th, 1969. Is that what's right? Yeah, that's right. And we're interviewing Shirley George's daughter at 3rd 3rd 27th, the Arnold Street. Just a second time. Okay, well Shirley, tell me about your, let's say, early memories or earliest memories around, I guess that was the time when you were around on St. Philip Street. Would that be right? Yeah.

Do you remember that time? That would be about right. That's when my now and Jeffries met Bill Russell. Yeah. He and a couple of other guys, I don't know their name offhand, came to the house and, um, he didn't believe in banks. He asked my mother to keep his money for him. A lot of them spent the night on the floor. And I understand that was when they made the recording of the Bundy Street Blues in the backyard. And then, um, Lawrence. Who? Lawrence. Yeah, and Uncle Lawrence to me. And, um, Slow Drake, Mr. Jim Robinson. I don't know if he was playing drum at the time. Well, what do you, how do you remember Bill Russell at that time? Well, I was one who didn't care to eat very much.
And, um, he and Ron Johnson used to kid me a lot.

And Lisa was one who didn't care to eat very much. And, um, he and Ron Johnson used to kid me a lot. At least, Ron did anyway, about eating my food all the time. Every time my mother would fix it, I wouldn't eat it. And he'd say, well, he was going to eat my food. So, between the two of them, they coaxed me into eating. And, um, I don't know, I just more or less took to Bill Russell. And from that time on up until now, every Christmas, he sends me my Christmas card with a $5 bill in it. And, I don't know, I just liked it, and I just took to him from a child.
What about Bump? Do you remember Bump in those days very much?

No, except for him wanting to eat my food all the time. That's why the only thing I can remember. He wanted to eat it? I didn't want to eat it. He figured if he said he'd eat it, I'd eat. Oh, I see. I'd get mad and want to eat. But, uh, that's about all I can recall from, Johnston.
Can you remember what he looked like?

Well, to me, him and Thomas Valentin, they resemble a lot. Yes, yeah, they look much alike. They look much alike. Uh-huh. Bill Russell said that too, right? They do. I think that maybe both was a little taller, but, uh, they look very much alike. Uh-huh.
What about, what are your memories of George at that time? Or what, was he working on the dock stand?

Yeah, yeah. Uh, he worked there in the daytime and he worked, uh, at night. I don't know if it was every night during that time, but I remember him very well. He worked there every day. Uh, cause I can remember him trying to work on his bicycle. Uh, when he'd come home in the evening, I'd be sitting outside the front door waiting for him. And I can remember him paddling down the street on his red and white bicycle. On his what? Red and white bicycle. Yeah. But, uh, I know he was working at night, but I don't know if it was regular work at night. But the riverfront, I remember very well.
Did he go down to the riverfront every day? Oh, yes. So you sort of had a regular job? Yeah, that was regular.
Because even after we moved over here in 52, he went back on the riverfront.
Oh, he did that, didn't he? Oh, yeah. After 52?
Yeah. Because, uh, I think it was a week after we moved over here, uh, El Morocco closed down and he just went back on the riverfront. Oh, really?
Uh-huh. He was playing at El Morocco his latest, that was it? Uh-huh. Can you remember, can you by any chance remember the month when you moved over here?

Oh, yes. It was March the 2nd, 1952. On a Sunday. Very good. And I remember them a lot because, um, I had to go to church that morning and, um, Mass was from the 830. And after Mass, um, I had to go back to the house to pick up something. And when I came over by myself, that's how I remember it was a Sunday, but it was March the 2nd.
Where had you been living before, just before you came here? Where did you live from?
On Dauphin Street. I think it was 18, 19, Dauphin.
Oh, yeah.

Yeah. And we stayed there for five years. Why did George want to move over here? Do you know? Well, all of my mother's relatives were over here. And I think it was about two years before we moved that they purchased a lot. He wasn't too particular, but my mother always wanted a house of her own. And one morning, he was going to see his mother. And the three of us walked through the alley to the front. And there was a big for sale sign on the house. And it upset my mother very much because she had her trouble. So it was then that they decided to build.
He sort of actually helped to build it. Or I gather wasn't it Drag and Lawrence had something to do with that.

Yeah. They put the baseboards up and the frames in the house. They did that and the doors. The windows. Yeah. I think they put the windows up too. Oh. Yeah, between him and Uncle Lawrence and, it was mostly Uncle Lawrence, no drag helped when he could, but between him and Uncle Lawrence and my mother, they did the rest. She contributed a lot to it.
You call, you refer to Uncle Lawrence, did you think of him as an uncle?
Yes, by him and my father being very close. So, from what I understand, when I first started walking, he said, come to Uncle Lawrence, and from then on, it's been Uncle Lawrence.
Did you know him very well, Lawrence? Did you get to know him very well?
Well, I'd say pretty well.
I can imagine, he had died before I got to him.

Oh, yeah. Well, he and my father were pretty close, and his wife and my mother were close, but not as close as the two of them. And they used to call each other brother-in-law. And he'd come to the house a lot, and my mother and father would go to his house a lot. Yeah, they were very close.

Tell me some, most of the things, of course, about George and the book. Probably about music and that kind of thing. But I was wondering if you could fill me in on some things which wouldn't be to do with music, like to some other aspects. Like, for instance, did George like to cook? Oh, yes. Can you tell me about that? I mean, anything you can think of about that would be interesting.

Well, next to music, he loved cooking. He liked gourmet food. And he wasn't one to go for leftovers. If he cooked a lot of food today, he had to cook tomorrow because he enjoyed cooking. He just loved to have a lot of food in the house. Unfortunately, that was one thing I didn't take after him. I can cook, but I don't like to cook as much as he did. And he cooked a lot of Creole dishes. He had a cookbook. It's called the White House Cookbook. He wanted to run through it to find a few other recipes that he had more or less forgot. But he didn't get a chance to get to the cookbook.
Can you tell me some of the things he actually cooked and some of the ideas he had about cooking?

Well, let's see. Okra gumbo he loved when the season was around. And feely gumbo, raisins naturally. And cabbage. Well, those were the food things that we would have. Well, he liked to bake roasts and ducks. And they call these little things, these pigs. Suckling pigs. Yeah, he liked that. And geese. He just enjoyed preparing the food.
Did he have any particular ways of doing it that was special to him?
No, no, no special way of doing it. As far as measuring things, he never did that. He just would throw it in. Nice. Yeah, a lot of spice.
Alan Jaffey somewhere around has a tape, which he's never been able to find. I guess he would find it sometime. George telling ghost stories. Did he ever tell ghost stories much?

Well, occasionally, but most of the time if he was going to tell, you know, it'd be after 10 o'clock. And some of my friends would be over and we'd start talking. Well, some would have to go on the corner around the corner. And they didn't want to hear it because they were afraid to go home. But he enjoyed telling tales and stories. But I never was one to sit down and really pay attention because I was kind of afraid myself. You were kind of what? Afraid.
Afraid. Afraid. Well, do you think he believed in this?
Well, that's kind of hard to answer. I would just say he actually believed in it, but some of the things he said that has happened will more or less make you stop and wonder.
Can you remember any of the things? Can you tell me some of the things he said?

Well, one particular story I remember very well was a man, he liked to gamble a lot. And his mother was Creole and she used to always scold him when he'd stay out late for gambling. And she used to sigh a lot, take a deep breath. So he just kept on gambling and eventually his mother got sick and she died. So he said it was one night late, about two or three in the morning, a man was coming home. And he had to cross over a little bridge like, and he saw this lady leaning over the bridge. So the man walked up to her and told her, don't jump. You know, things couldn't be that bad. So he said, the lady still was leaning on the rail and she didn't look up. She just took a deep sigh. And it scared him because that's what his mother used to always do. And he believed that that was his mother.
What was the story that you told me that you saw something like?

Oh, well, we used to sit in the back door on Safeville Street. I'd see a man and a lady and a little girl and a little boy and a dog walking the fence. Well, a lot of people, the fence, you know, dividing the yard. Well, the neighbors used to tell my mother, they don't see how she could stay with me. You know, they felt that she should have been afraid. But she said, no, she wasn't afraid. But I used to see her more all the time. As I got older, I guess I'm more or less groggy. But I'd sit in the back door and I'd talk to her. And they'd talk to me. And she'd be in the kitchen cooking and she'd ask me who I was talking to. And I'd tell her, man, a lady on the fence.
So they'd be on the fence? Yeah.
They'd be walking the fence. Walking on top of that? Mm-hmm. And your mother couldn't see it? No.
No, she couldn't see it, but she wasn't frightened.
How old were you when that was? Let's say about three or four.
Did you tell George about that? Yes. No, they weren't frightened. They didn't see it. They were afraid of the people. They were afraid of the people. They were afraid of the people.

They were afraid of the people. They were afraid of the people. They weren't frightened. They didn't doubt me, but they more or less pampered me until I stopped seeing them. Because I tried to show it to my mother. And she'd say, yeah, she'd see it. She'd say, yeah, baby, mama, see the lady. And as I got older and I'd ask her about it, she said, no, she didn't see it. But she was afraid to say she didn't see it for fear it might frighten me. What about voodoo? Was George interested in that at all?
No, I wouldn't say he was interested in that. Didn't pay any attention to it? No. I gather there was a lot of it when he was a boy growing up. But to say believe in it, no, no he didn't.

Because my grandmother was a very strict Catholic and she brought him up to be the same way. And you couldn't believe in both. No. And I didn't say he was interested in that. Didn't say he was interested in that. Didn't pay any attention to it? No. I gather there was a lot of it when he was a boy growing up. But to say believe in it, no, no he didn't. Because my grandmother was a very strict Catholic and she brought him up to be the same way. And you couldn't believe in both. No. So he believed in his religion, but not voodoo. Tell me about your grandmother and what you remember of her. Well, she and I weren't very close at all. Until after my mother died, she moved over here. She was more or less my guardian while my daddy was out of town. But at the time she was too old to be a guardian for a teenage girl. But that's when we more or less got kind of close and she moved over here. But as a child I used to go and see her every day. And on Sundays especially.
Where did she live then?
She lived 910 St. Philip Street. It was in the next block from us. And a one room apartment.
What was that for any particular striking romance or interest?

Well, she was another one who liked to cook. But age wouldn't permit it. But she tried her best to cook. Especially on Sundays. She felt that you should have a big meal and you should have some kind of dessert. And while she was over here, she tried to do it until one morning her gown caught a fire. So we more or less forbid her to put the stove after that. But she was a quiet person. She stayed to herself a lot. Because she used to pray a lot. She'd lay across her bed and see the rosemary's all the time. And she liked to watch television. Well, when she came over here that was her first time seeing television. And she'd watch the news and she'd watch Midday. And after that she didn't bother with television anymore. And these people would come to see her. She'd talk to them for about maybe, if she lasted a half an hour. And she'd just get up and go in her room. If she was on the telephone, I can remember one time she was talking to somebody. And it went for a long conversation and she felt she had talked long enough. She just put the phone down and walked off and got in the bed. She didn't say bye or anything. She didn't believe in holding up the phone that long. See what she had to say and get it over with.
Do you, um, let me ask you something about Jordan. Do you remember him practicing at all? Did he practice around the place? No.

Um, sometimes he'd pick up the horn. And if he wanted to fix a pad or something on it. And after he had glued the pad on or whatever you do to the pad, he'd blow it a while. But for the same practice, no, he never practiced. For the same practice, no, he didn't do that. Because a lot of children would come and they'd find it strange but while he did, they don't practice. So, you know, playing is all. If he hadn't played in a while to get his fingers in order, but for the same practice, no, he didn't do that. Because a lot of children would come and they'd find it strange, but while you're dead, they don't practice. You know, playing is all. I say, well, he's been with it a long time, and I don't guess he feels he has to practice. You know, he didn't practice and he didn't read music, and that was kind of strange to some people. I would say he could play so well and couldn't read music.
Did he ever talk about music or saying anything about his ideas about music or anything like that?

His ideas about music. Well, he liked music of all types. He didn't down any type music. But jazz was his love. All he wanted to do was to play and to play well. But for the same, he had any ideas about it. If he did, he didn't mention it. He just wanted to play his horn because he loved playing his horn and he enjoyed it very much.
When did you first start action? Let me say, when did you first hear that?
